Photograph: Eduardo Barraza/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock Al Gore Passing bill to speed up gas projects and datacenters would be ‘serious mistake’, Al Gore says Former US vice-president at Cop31 urges lawmakers to rethink contentious bipartisan Baaja bill advanced by the US Senate Oliver Milman in Antalya, Turkey Mon 16 Nov 2026 09.34 EST Last modified on Mon 16 Nov 2026 13.07 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google It would be a “serious mistake” to pass a contentious bipartisan bill to speed up energy projects and datacenters that has divided Democrats and environmentalists, Al Gore said. The legislation, known as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (Baaja), will make it easier to build large infrastructure projects in the US, from oil and gas pipelines and datacenters to crucial clean energy components such as solar and wind power and transmission lines, scaling back environmental protections and legal challenges in order to do so. The permitting bill, devised by a group of Republicans and Democrats, passed a procedural vote in the US Senate last week , but has split Democrats and green groups over whether its trade-offs are worth supporting. pages.title: Pat Cummins calls Usman Khawaja sandpaper claims 'wrong' and 'nonsense' - BBC Sport
pages.description: Australia captain Pat Cummins hits back at former team-mate Usman Khawaja’s claims over the sandpaper scandal, calling them “100% wrong” and “utter nonsense”.
pages.text: Pat Cummins calls Usman Khawaja sandpaper claims 'wrong' and 'nonsense' - BBC Sport Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Pat Cummins was named Australia Test captain in 2021 By Stephan Shemilt Cricket Correspondent Published 12 November 2026 Updated 13 November 2026 Australia captain Pat Cummins has hit back at former team-mate Usman Khawaja's claims over the sandpaper scandal, calling them "100% wrong" and "utter nonsense". In 2018, Steve Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft were punished for a plot to tamper with the ball using sandpaper in Australia's Test against South Africa in Cape Town. Khawaja has published his autobiography this week and the former batter has said the entire Australia team, which included Cummins, knew about the sandpaper scheme and should have taken responsibility. But in an extraordinary 68-minute address to the media in Sydney, Cummins countered and said: "When he says we all knew, if by that he means we knew sandpaper was going out on the field, he's 100% wrong. "I said that consistently for the last eight years. I did not know that was happening. "He says that I and others were architects of a scheme to ball tamper with sandpaper. That's complete and utter nonsense." Figure caption, Complete and utter nonsense - Cummins Cummins and Khawaja played 56 Tests together until Khawaja retired from international cricket in January. Khawaja was in the Australia XI when Cummins made his Test debut in 2011 and the pair were also once team-mates in domestic cricket with New South Wales. pages.text: Pat McFadden backs legal right to job support for young people Skip to content Site search Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Weather Newsletters Watch Live Minister backs legal right to job support for young people 1 day ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Paul Seddon Political reporter Watch: Pat McFadden refuses to rule out that some young people might lose benefits The work and pensions secretary has backed the idea that the government should legally guarantee young people help to get into employment. Pat McFadden told the BBC that job support should be given a "legislative underpinning", adding the level of assistance on offer was currently "vague". McFadden also confirmed that some current benefit claimants would see their current entitlement to benefits reduced when they are reassessed. But his Conservative counterpart Helen Whately said the idea of legally guaranteeing support "doesn't make sense" and ministers should focus instead on reducing taxes paid by employers. It comes ahead of a long-awaited review by former Labour cabinet minister Alan Milburn, which will recommend on Tuesday that under-25s should be guaranteed job placements or training to help them find permanent work. His report is also expected to say that under-25s should no longer be able to claim the health element of UK-wide universal credit - or personal independence payment (Pip), the main disability benefit in England and Wales. This program allows employers to correct mistakes efficiently and ensure employees receive back wages or other remedies promptly, all while avoiding litigation. Under PAID, employers are encouraged to conduct audits and, if they discover FLSA or FMLA violations, to self-report those violations. Employers may then work in good faith with WHD to correct their mistakes and to quickly provide 100% of the back wages due or other remedies to their affected employees. pages.text: Peace Corps Volunteers | U.S. Department of Labor Skip to main content Peace Corps Volunteers Federal Employees’ Compensation Program A Peace Corps Volunteer who sustains an injury or illness in performance of their Peace Corps service may be entitled to benefits under the Federal Employees' Compensation Act (FECA). The FECA, administered by the Department's Office of Workers' Compensation Programs (OWCP), provides medical, wage loss and other compensation benefits for Peace Corps Volunteers who sustain injury or illness while in the performance of duty. Peace Corps Volunteers are considered to be in the performance of duty while abroad during the period of Peace Corps service for purposes of FECA coverage. An injury sustained outside the United States is deemed proximately caused by such service, unless the injury or illness was caused by willful misconduct, intention to bring about injury or death, or intoxication. FECA benefits may also be provided for an injury or illness present prior to entering Peace Corps service, if evidence supports that Peace Corps service contributed to a worsening of the condition. The Peace Corps provides medical and dental care that covers all related expenses during service, including preventative care and issues incurred during training period. Until you are separated from the Peace Corps, you are encouraged to seek medical and dental care from the Peace Corps . People at Increased Risk for Food Poisoning Jan. 31, 2025 Key points Certain groups of people are at higher risk for severe illness from foodborne illness. Higher risk groups include people who are 65 and older, children under 5, people with weakened immune systems, and pregnant women. People at increased risk Anyone can get food poisoning, but certain groups of people are more likely to get very sick from food poisoning. For these people, their body may not be able to fight germs and sickness as effectively. It's especially important to take steps to prevent food poisoning if you or someone you care for belong to one of the groups below. People 65 and older People aged 65 and older are at increased risk for food poisoning. As people age, their immune systems and organs don't recognize and get rid of harmful germs as well as they once did. This increases the chance they'll get sick from food poisoning. Nearly half of people aged 65 and older who have a lab-confirmed foodborne illness from Salmonella , Campylobacter , Listeria or E. coli are hospitalized. Riskier animals include rodents, reptiles, amphibians, and poultry. These people don't need to avoid all contact with animals but should be aware of the risks and take steps to protect themselves. High-risk animals Turtles can carry germs that can make some people very sick. These animals are more likely to carry germs that can make people sick: Reptiles and amphibians (lizards, snakes, turtles, frogs) Backyard poultry (chickens, ducks, turkeys, geese) Rodents (hamsters, guinea pigs, rats, mice, and other small rodents) Exotic pets (monkeys and other wild animals) Even animals that look clean and healthy can carry harmful germs, and areas where animals live or roam can be contaminated – you don’t have to touch an animal to get sick. NPS / Tahzay Jones Many parts of Alaska have a hidden underground world of frozen ground. The depth and extent of this “permafrost” varies by location, depending on average air temperatures, soil types, topography, and surface vegetation. Frozen ground is stable, providing a solid foundation for roads and buildings. Permafrost is also impermeable, so water pools on the surface instead of seeping through the soil, and creates a landscape dotted with many small lakes. The shorter and warmer winters are affecting permafrost. – Dave Swanson, Fairbanks Rising temperatures are melting this frozen ground and forever altering the landscape. Without this solid foundation, roads and buildings sink into the softer, non-frozen ground. Sinkholes and slumpages form when their frozen supportive underground layers thaw. And lakes previously formed by permafrost have begun to drain. Melting Permafrost Shifting sands of coastal barrier islands. pages.text: Personal Assistance Services | U.S. Department of Labor Skip to main content Personal Assistance Services More in This Section Close Accessible Technology Communications Access Health Care Housing Personal Assistance Services Transportation Universal Design For many individuals with disabilities, personal assistance services (PAS) help make employment possible. Some people use PAS to carry out activities of daily living. Depending on the individual, such activities might include getting up and ready for work, bathing, dressing, cooking, cleaning, or running errands. Some people also use PAS in the workplace. Examples of workplace PAS vary, but may involve activities such as retrieving materials out of reach or providing travel assistance for an employee with a mobility impairment; helping an employee with a cognitive disability in decision-making; reading printed materials to an employee who is visually impaired; or ensuring a sign language interpreter is present during meetings for an employee who is deaf. Whether at home or work, PAS can be essential to employment success. Recognizing this, ODEP works to expand and raise awareness of employment-related PAS options. Meeting the needs of people on and off the job raises important policy issues for federal and state governments, service providers, and employers, as well as people with disabilities themselves. ODEP recognizes PAS is a critical issue — not only for those seeking employment, but also for those already employed. History In 2010, a paper map by 3dShapes was digitized and imported, to map landuse in Nederland. The import project was well conducted and properly documented in the OSM-wiki. This was a major step in filling in the space on OSM. Some problems remained after import, to be dealt with later. For instance, where trees had been planted in multiple rows, it was imported as an orchard. As a result, our motorways were suddenly lined with orchards, on OSM-based maps. This has been fixed by organized mappings. Another example: the paper map had a tile grid of thin black lines. These lines were seen as cut lines, resulting in unnecessary and awkward splits of the imported areas. The import procedure did detect this problem, but couldn’t automate a fix, so this was left to the future mappers. It took 15 years before a crazy mapper got rid of this in a solo project lasting 2 months. Guess who? The issue Not much of a problem, more of an annoyance, really: All polygons were tagged with “source=3dShapes”. A significant part of the polygons still carry this source tag. Skip to content Site search Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Weather Newsletters Watch Live What is PHP and why did it spark a global cyber-security scramble? 23 October 2026 Share Save Add as preferred on Google Liv McMahon , Technology reporter and Osmond Chia , Business reporter How did AI discover the internet's massive cyber-security risk? For more than a decade, serious flaws had gone undetected in the technology underpinning much of the internet. It took AI to bring them to light and caused a global cyber-security alert. Researchers who helped surface the vulnerabilities in PHP - a popular server-side programming language used in web development for decades - warned platforms which use it could be exposed to potential hacks. Governments and cyber-security agencies rushed to contain the fallout , urging website owners to check if their sites were affected and, if so, install updates to patch the issue or consider going offline. There have been no reports of any successful exploits of the flaw, coined php2shell, so far. But in the days since the issues came to light, disruption to sites and services has continued to ripple around the world. What is PHP? Most people may not have heard of PHP, but they probably interact with it daily. It stands for PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor, an open-source, back-end programming language which runs on a web server. Located approximately 100 miles (161 km) northeast of Fairbanks, this 27-mile (44 km) hiking trail traverses a series of alpine ridge tops entirely above timberline. The trail was built for hikers, but is open to all forms of non-motorized use. The Pinnell Mountain Trail is marked with rock cairns as it crosses open tundra with views north to the Yukon River and south to the Alaska Range. Wooden posts along the trail show the mileage from the start at Eagle Summit to the trail's end at Twelvemile Summit. Two shelters provide refuge from storms, but hikers should come prepared for unpredictable, dramatic alpine weather. Search Twitter YouTube Facebook Instagram Flickr LinkedIn Canyons of the Ancients National Monument | Colorado View Map In Full Screen Canyons of the Ancients National Monument, located in the Four Corners region of southwestern Colorado, protects a stunning cultural landscape with the highest known density of archaeological sites in the United States. Encompassing 176,000 acres of public lands, the Monument features more than 8,300 documented sites—including villages, kivas, field houses, cliff dwellings, petroglyphs, and ancient roadways—with estimates suggesting over 30,000 yet to be recorded. These sites offer a window into over 12,000 years of human history, primarily shaped by Ancestral Puebloan cultures and their descendants. The area continues to be a living landscape used today for traditional purposes, recreation, hunting, livestock grazing, and energy development. It also encompasses Cross Canyon , Sego Lily, and Cahone Canyon Wilderness Study Areas. While exploring the Monument’s canyons, mesas, and desert terrain, visitors are reminded to Visit with Respect and Leave No Trace to protect the resources that define this unique place. Search Twitter YouTube Facebook Instagram Flickr LinkedIn Agua Fria National Monument | Arizona View Map In Full Screen Plan Your Visit Visitors to Agua Fria National Monument can hike in rugged landscapes, view rock art, and experience wide‑open desert vistas with few built facilities. Because the area is remote and minimally serviced, visitors should plan ahead and be prepared for changing weather and rough roads. Things to Do Hike and explore : Walk sandy washes and rocky routes to river corridors and mesa‑top dwellings. Trails are mostly undeveloped; carry plenty of water and wear sturdy footwear. View cultural sites : Visit mesa‑top pueblos and petroglyph panels. Look, photograph, and leave artifacts in place. But in 2001, a thriving population was found on land south of Santiago Photograph By SELECTPHOTO/ALAMY STOCK PHOTO ENVIRONMENT VANISHING Plant extinctions are shaking Earth’s green foundation Compared with birds, mammals, and amphibians, more plants have vanished in the wild since 1900. What’s the cost to ecosystems? By Michael Greshko 3 min read This story appears in the October 2019 issue of National Geographic magazine. When you conjure up “extinction” in your mind’s eye, you probably see an animal—a dodo , perhaps, or a Tasmanian tiger . But the biodiversity crisis isn’t just faunal, it’s floral too. Since the 1750s, at least 571 species of plants have gone extinct in the wild, according to a global survey recently published in Nature Ecology & Evolution . More than eight plant species have disappeared every three years, on average, since 1900. pages.text: Polar Bears in the Roman Colosseum? | National Geographic By Candida Moss Published September 28, 2026 Want to make sure you get every Stones & Bones newsletter? Put your email here . There’s a strange and intriguing reference in the writings of a first-century Roman poet who describes a showdown between bears and seals (or, as he called them, “sea-calves”) in the Colosseum. Only polar bears are known to fight seals, so this raises a question no modern scholar has yet been able to answer: How on Earth would arctic bears have traveled to the heart of the Roman Empire? A clue to the ursine mystery has recently emerged—in the first English language book on Scandinavian Roman-era history, Dagfinn Skre's The Northern Routes to Kingshi p . Skre places Sweden, Norway, and Denmark at the periphery of the empire, showing that Denmark was only a four-week march from the Roman frontier. And in fact, the Roman military was recruiting from the region by the late first century A.D. So the social networks and infrastructure were in place to facilitate the movement of exotic animals that Rome craved for its spectacles. I reached out to Michael Kulikowski, a professor of classics at Penn State who wrote about Skre’s work for the London Review of Books , for more on how polar bears could have ended up on the sands of Rome’s most famous arena. pages.description: It was one of history’s most dramatic moments—but the eruption of Mount Vesuvius wasn’t a single disaster. Recent evidence reveals how three settlements faced three distinct fates, reshaping our understanding of how ancient Romans lived and died.
pages.text: Pompeii's Secrets: How AI is Rewriting the Story of Mount Vesuvius | National Geographic By Sam Kean Photographs by Paolo Verzone Video by Massimo Nicolaci Published July 23, 2026 Outside, the world was vanishing. A scum of ash was thickening on the surface of the Gulf of Naples, and black fumes were swallowing the sky above. In a waterfront warehouse in the Roman town of Oplontis, five dozen people cowered in terror. Some clutched gold coins and jewelry—family wealth snatched up in panic. Others gripped common iron tools and little more. One young woman hugged her swollen belly, terrified for the unborn child inside. Their ages and social classes varied widely, but they’d likely all gathered in a storeroom on the water’s edge for the same reason: to await a rescue boat they were increasingly fearful would never come. In A.D. 79, Mount Vesuvius blew its top, raining ash over the Campania region of Italy, near modern-day Naples, and burying surrounding communities beneath as much as 60 feet of volcanic debris. What happened that day in A.D. 79 began with a single event, the eruption of Mount Vesuvius . But each settlement in the volcano’s shadow—including the most famous, Pompeii —experienced a distinct catastrophe depending on its location relative to the volcano and the timing, speed, and direction of the material Vesuvius spewed. A handful of lucky folks within those communities escaped.
